newsitem.title: UK: London loses mark repo business but unfazed so far.
newsitem.headline: London loses mark repo business but unfazed so far.

text.p: The City of London, working hard to retain its dominance as a European financial centre, was dealt a minor blow on Wednesday when two top German banks said they would take their securities repurchase business in marks back to Frankfurt.
Aside from the symbolic impact of surrendering business to its main European rival, London will have to count the cost of losing an important share of trade in a burgeoning sector.
"It was substantial. All the repo business was done out of London for Europe. The German repo stuff was a hefty chunk of that," said one source familiar with trade in this market.
Deutsche Bank AG and Commerzbank AG both announced on Wednesday that they would bring their mark repo business to Frankfurt. Of the two, Deutsche Bank is said to be the bigger player in this market.
Both cited the recent decision by the Bundesbank to exempt some repo business from reserve requirements as the main reason for the move.

Repo operations supply liquidity to the bond markets. A repo business is basically a bank's operations in lending securities to investors who need those securities for short periods of time to conduct their own trades.

Typically a trader wanting to "short" a security will borrow it from a repo desk, sell it in the market on the view it will go down in value, then buy it back later and return it to the repo desk. If the security does in fact go down in price, the cost to buy it back will be less than what the trader sold it for, and the deal will have made money.
But because of costly reserve requirements, German banks in the past have opted to conduct their repo trade out London, even if their mark-denominated debt trading was in Frankfurt.

A large amount of German bank trading operations are in London, following moves in recent years to concentrate most non-mark business in one European centre. London is the largest foreign exchange centre in Europe by far and also is home to markets such as Eurobonds and syndicate loans.

In terms of tradeable debt, mark issues make up the biggest share among Continental European markets, according to figures cited by one source. France is a close second but other markets in Europe were generally half as big or smaller.

A London banking industry source said that aside from the Bundesbank's reserve requirement decision, the move also might make sense in terms of the introduction of the euro currency under European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
What are now mark repo deals are due to become euro repo deals in the future, and that can mean cheap intraday liquidity under EMU for these banks, he said.
"That (repo business) would all be collateralised. They can borrow against that and pay virtually no interest on it," the industry source said.
In other words, these banks can borrow funds in euros, using repo deals they have conducted as collateral.
